title: Space Complexity
description: How algorithms consume memory -- **input space** vs **auxiliary space**, and the **time-space tradeoffs** engineers navigate constantly.

activities.title: Checking if a List is Empty

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Every lesson so far has asked one question: *how long does this take?* This lesson asks a different one: *how much memory does this need?*

Time complexity asks **how long**. Space complexity asks **how much RAM**. They're measured the same way -- in Big-O, as a function of input size `n` -- but they're tracking two genuinely different resources, and an algorithm can be excellent at one while being terrible at the other.

subsections.title: Time vs Space
subsections.content: A program that crashes from running out of memory has failed just as completely as one that's too slow to be useful -- it just fails in a different, sometimes more sudden way. You'll see both kinds of failure in this course, and it's worth being able to diagnose which one you're looking at.

subsections.title: The Balancing Act
subsections.content: Caching speeds up repeated work but can grow to gigabytes if left unchecked. Recomputing instead of storing uses less memory but runs slower. There's rarely a free lunch -- and recognizing that tradeoff, rather than being surprised by it later, is most of what this lesson is really teaching.

subsections.title: Answering Important Questions
subsections.content: Space complexity answers questions like:
bullets: Will this run on a phone with **limited memory**?
Will this recursive function **stack overflow**?
Is extra memory worth it to make this **faster**?

sections.title: Why Space Complexity Matters
sections.content: RAM is limited -- phones might have 4-8 GB, smartwatches just kilobytes, and even servers need careful management running thousands of tasks at once.

subsections.title: Consequences of Poor Management
subsections.content: Poor memory habits cause real failures:
bullets: Loading millions of records at once can **crash the system**.
Uncompressed images eat gigabytes fast.
Deep, unoptimized recursion causes **stack overflow**.

subsections.title: Real-World Architecture
subsections.content: Streaming services process video in **small chunks**, not whole files. APIs paginate -- 100 records at a time, not a million.

bullets: **Design systems** that stay stable with large datasets.
**Optimize memory** in constrained environments.
**Avoid unnecessary copying** of large structures.
**Spot hidden costs** from recursion or helper structures.

sections.title: Understanding Space Complexity
sections.content: **Space complexity** measures total memory needed relative to input size `n`.

subsections.title: What it Includes
subsections.content: Counts toward space:
bullets: **Local variables**
**Temporary storage**
**Recursion stack memory**
**Helper structures** like new arrays or dicts

subsections.title: Using Big-O Notation
subsections.content: Same Big-O classes as time:
bullets: **O(1)** -- a few tracking variables.
**O(n)** -- e.g. copying the input array.
**O(n²)** -- e.g. an n×n matrix.

chart.title: Memory growth relative to input size
chart.description: Constant, linear, and quadratic space -- how fast auxiliary memory grows as n increases.

sections.title: Input Space vs Auxiliary Space
sections.content: Two different kinds of memory to keep straight:

subsections.title: Input Space
subsections.content: **Input space** is the memory already required just to hold the input, before the algorithm does anything.

subsections.title: Auxiliary Space
subsections.content: **Auxiliary space** is the *extra* memory the algorithm creates -- temp arrays, helper dicts, recursion frames, local variables.

subsections.title: The Engineering Focus
subsections.content: Engineers usually mean **auxiliary space** when they say "O(1) space" -- the overhead the implementation adds, not the unavoidable cost of the input itself.

sections.title: Constant Space: O(1)
sections.content: Memory usage that doesn't grow with input size -- the algorithm might read a huge input but only ever holds a fixed number of extra variables.

subsections.title: A Classic Example
subsections.content: Finding the max in a list needs just **one tracking variable** -- true whether the list has 10 items or 10 million.

subsections.title: Common O(1) Operations
subsections.content: Also O(1) space:
bullets: Summing with an accumulator.
Checking if a number is prime.
Swapping two variables with one temp variable.

subsections.title: Why it Matters
subsections.content: Critical for memory-constrained devices -- if you can process data without storing all of it, you can handle unbounded input with fixed memory.

codeSnippets.title: Find a maximum with O(1) auxiliary space

sections.title: Linear Space: O(n)
sections.content: Auxiliary memory grows in proportion to input size -- double the input, roughly double the extra memory.

subsections.title: The Copying Problem
subsections.content: Copying a 1-million-item array needs another 1 million items' worth of memory -- **doubling** total usage.

subsections.title: The Memory Overhead of Array Slicing
subsections.content: Slicing looks lightweight but actually allocates a new array and copies the elements into it -- **O(n)** space, not free.

subsections.title: Common O(n) Operations
subsections.content: Also O(n) space:
bullets: Storing all messages to display later.
Building a `Set` of unique elements.
A results list with one output per input.

subsections.title: Scale and Limitations
subsections.content: Fine at moderate n (thousands), risky at hundreds of millions -- always weigh space against your expected input size.

codeSnippets.title: Copying a list creates O(n) extra space
codeSnippets.code:
def copy_values(values):
    copied = []

    for value in values:
        copied.append(value)

    return copied

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(copy_values(numbers))

sections.title: Quadratic Space: O(n^2)
sections.content: Memory grows with the square of n -- common with grids and matrices where both dimensions scale with n.

subsections.title: The Exponential Cost of Grids
subsections.content: An n×n matrix has n² cells:
bullets: n = 1,000 → 1M cells (~8 MB).
n = 100,000 → 10 billion cells (**~80 GB** -- too much for most systems).

subsections.title: Common O(n²) Examples
subsections.content: Graph adjacency matrices, edit-distance DP tables, all-pairs distance matrices.

codeSnippets.title: An n by n matrix uses O(n^2) space
codeSnippets.code:
def create_matrix(n):
    matrix = []

    for row in range(n):
        matrix.append([0] * n)

    return matrix

board = create_matrix(4)
print(board)

sections.title: Recursion and Stack Memory
sections.content: One of the most overlooked memory costs: every recursive call creates a stack frame holding its own local variables and return info.

subsections.title: Stack Growth
subsections.content: Frames stick around until the call returns -- space complexity is typically **O(depth)**, even with no arrays involved.

subsections.title: The Stack Overflow Crash
subsections.content: Python's default recursion limit is ~1,000 frames -- go past it and you get a **Stack Overflow**. Save recursion for cases with small or logarithmic depth.

codeSnippets.title: Recursive countdown uses O(n) stack frames

sections.title: Recursive vs Iterative Solutions
sections.content: Recursive code is often shorter and closer to the math. Iterative code (loops) is usually more memory-efficient.

subsections.title: Example: Binary Search
subsections.content: Recursive binary search uses **O(log n)** stack space. The iterative version skips the stack entirely -- **O(1)**.

subsections.title: Making the Choice
subsections.content: Processing a 100,000-item linked list recursively needs 100,000 stack frames -- a guaranteed crash. The iterative version needs O(1) space. Always check the max recursion depth before choosing.

codeSnippets.title: Iterative binary search uses O(1) auxiliary space

sections.title: In-Place Algorithms
sections.content: An **in-place algorithm** modifies the input directly instead of building large new structures -- critical for large datasets on limited memory.

subsections.title: Micro-Transition: Stepping Into Array Mutations
subsections.content: Practice mutating a list in place -- removing an item or sorting it -- so you learn to change data efficiently without accidentally doubling your memory use.

subsections.title: What is In-Place?
subsections.content: Uses **O(1) auxiliary space** -- maybe a temp variable for swapping, but never a new array.

subsections.title: Common Examples
subsections.content: In-place operations:
bullets: Swapping two elements.
Reversing an array from the edges inward.
Bubble, selection, and insertion sort.

subsections.title: Pros and Cons
subsections.content: Less memory, faster allocation, better cache use -- but it **destroys the original data**, which is a dealbreaker if you need to keep it.

codeSnippets.title: Swap values in place
codeSnippets.code:
values = [10, 20, 30, 40]

# Swap two positions without creating another list.
values[1], values[3] = values[3], values[1]
print(values)

sections.title: Time vs Space Tradeoffs
sections.content: There's no perfect algorithm -- faster usually costs memory, and memory-lean usually costs speed. This is the **Time-Space Tradeoff**.

subsections.title: In-Place Deletion and Memory Shifts
subsections.content: Deleting from the middle of an array in place is **O(1) space** -- but shifting every following element forward costs **O(n) time**. A classic tradeoff.

subsections.title: Caching (Memoization)
subsections.content: Caching trades **O(n) space** for a drop from exponential to linear time -- a very common and very good trade.

subsections.title: Dynamic Programming
subsections.content: DP tables store intermediate results to avoid repeat work -- sometimes you can keep just the last few rows instead of the whole table, trading time back for space.

sections.title: Space Complexity of Common Algorithms
sections.content: Different approaches, very different memory footprints:

subsections.title: Searching and Sorting
subsections.content: Linear search: **O(1)**. Merge sort: **O(n)** for merging buffers. Bubble sort: **O(1)**, in-place, despite its slow O(n²) time.

subsections.title: Graph Algorithms
subsections.content: BFS: **O(V)** for its queue. DFS: **O(V)** stack space. Floyd-Warshall: **O(n²)** for its full distance table.

subsections.title: Misconception: Variables do not affect memory complexity
subsections.content: A few fixed variables are O(1) -- but a variable holding a growing array pushes space to O(n) or worse.

subsections.title: Misconception: Recursion only affects time complexity
subsections.content: Every active call needs a stack frame -- recursion depth `d` means at least **O(d)** space.

subsections.title: Misconception: Fast algorithms are always better
subsections.content: A very fast algorithm that needs too much memory may not even run. On massive datasets, a slightly slower, leaner algorithm can be the only workable choice.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: **Space complexity** measures memory growth relative to input size.
**Auxiliary space** is the extra memory beyond the input itself.
**Recursive algorithms** carry hidden stack memory cost.
**In-place algorithms** save memory but mutate the original data.
**Time-Space Tradeoffs** mean faster often costs more memory, and vice versa.
